Keywords: Just, And, This

Just now I laid my hand upon my chest
And felt my heart there, quivering. This must
Be one of the bad times. It quivers, I think,
With remorse and with exhaustion. Once I saw
A heart still beating in a documentary.
I was a very little girl, and the sight
Disgusted me. Throbbing and never ceasing,
My heart betrays me, and yet remains steadfast
And true—a thing of nature. The Earth, bleeding
Its very guts out on the sea floor, wearies me
With remorse and shame, and yet I must trust it,
For wealth is proven by how terribly
It devastates itself; and I am but
One symptom among billions of the wealth
Of Earth. A weariness restored by a passing
Spaceship, or an infinitude like fame,
Though more universal. I will have to miss
You, Earth; already I miss you. And yet
When I touch myself—whom I should not trust—
It is still only the heaviest, most jealous
Of feelings that bind me to you, like blood.

This is surely one of those difficult moments.
I believe it trembles from regret

# The Weight of the Body and the World

I press my hand against my chest and feel my heart quivering beneath my ribs. In this difficult moment, I read the sensation as more than mere muscle and blood—it becomes a physical confession of remorse, a trembling that speaks of exhaustion, as though the body itself is bearing the strain of everything I cannot say aloud.

I remember, as a child, watching a documentary that showed a beating heart. The sight disgusted me. Something about that raw, pulsing organ—so intimate and yet so alien—unsettled me deeply. It was my first encounter with the body's unvarnished biological reality, and even then I sensed a discomfort with the machinery that keeps us alive, the wet and relentless truth hidden beneath our skin.

That discomfort has never fully left me. To this day, my heart seems to both betray me and remain faithful. It quickens when I wish it still; it aches when I would rather feel nothing. And yet it never stops. In this contradiction lives a strange tension: I distrust this organ, this insistent rhythm, even as I depend upon its unstoppable loyalty. It is a force of nature I cannot command, only endure.

Perhaps this is why I find myself thinking of the Earth itself—of its devastation, and how that ruin has become, paradoxically, a kind of wealth. The planet spends itself with terrible abundance, consuming and destroying in the very act of creating. And I am only one small symptom among billions, a single quiver in a vast, self-destructive body. My private remorse is nothing beside the scale of that squandering.

Still, I cannot separate myself from it. Even as I mistrust my own flesh, I feel bound to the Earth by emotions as heavy and jealous as they are inescapable—feelings as intimate as the blood that moves through me. I belong to this world the way I belong to my own restless heart: reluctantly, distrustfully, and completely.
outputs.L4:
# On the Quivering Heart and the Body of the World

There is a moment, usually in the deep hours when sleep refuses to come, when the speaker becomes aware of the heart as a physical thing—not a metaphor, not a symbol scrawled across a valentine, but a fist of muscle laboring in the dark of the chest. It quivers. It stumbles. And in that irregular rhythm, something opens: a meditation that stretches from the smallest chamber of the body outward to the wounded surface of the Earth itself.

The poem begins in the flesh. Blood moves through the speaker's veins with a persistence that feels almost accusatory, as though the body were determined to continue whether or not the mind consents. Each heartbeat becomes a small reminder of finitude—every contraction is one closer to the last, and the speaker cannot help but count them, cannot help but feel the pulse as a kind of clock. This is where mortality enters, not as an abstraction but as sensation: the quiver, the flutter, the terrible awareness that the machinery keeping us alive is fragile, temporary, and utterly beyond our control.

But the poem refuses to remain inward-looking. The speaker turns, almost involuntarily, toward the planet. The devastation of the Earth—its scorched forests, its poisoned waters, its slow bleeding out under the weight of what we have done—mirrors the exhaustion in the speaker's own tired body. There is a doubling here, a recognition that the body and the world are made of the same vulnerable stuff, that both are running down, both are marked by wounds that will not heal. The speaker feels this correspondence as remorse: a heavy, sourceless shame that seems to rise from the very act of being alive, of consuming, of taking up space on a dying ground.

And yet the poem's central insight is a paradox. One might expect that exhaustion and shame would drive the speaker away from life, would loosen the grip of attachment. Instead, the opposite occurs. It is precisely in the moment of feeling most depleted, most implicated, most ashamed, that the speaker feels most bound—to the body, to the breath, to the trembling planet turning beneath them. Belonging, the poem suggests, is not born from ease or gratitude or wonder. It is born from complicity. We belong to the Earth because we have hurt it and cannot separate ourselves from that hurt. We belong to our bodies because they carry our fatigue, our failures, our accumulated regret.

The visceral imagery throughout—the insistence on blood, on the raw thud of the heartbeat, on the imagined landscapes of planetary ruin—works to collapse the distance between self and world. The reader is not permitted to observe from a safe remove. Instead, we are made to feel the pulse in our own throats, to sense the weight of shared damage in our own chests. This is the poem's method and its argument at once: that the things we most distrust in ourselves—our weariness, our guilt, our mortality—are not obstacles to love but its foundation.

In the end, the quivering heart becomes an emblem of everything the poem wants to say. It is fragile and it is faithful. It carries the fear of ending and the fact of continuing. It ties the speaker to the earth not through any lofty ideal but through the plain, stubborn, aching persistence of being alive in a body, on a world, that we have wounded and that wounds us in return. The poem leaves us there—not comforted exactly, but held: bound most deeply to life by the very things we would have thought would set us free.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in which a speaker touches their own chest, feels their heart quivering, and connects that physical sensation to grief, remorse, and love for a dying Earth.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Hand Knows**

I lay my palm flat against the shirt,
against the skin beneath it,
against the small animal caged there—
and feel it stutter,
a moth against a window,
wanting out, wanting in,
I can never tell which.

This is the trembling I inherited.
This is the quiver that says
*you are still here,
and so is the wreckage.*

Under my fingers, a rhythm
learned from tides,
from the slow breathing of forests
I have watched go gray,
from rivers I let thin
to a bright thread of themselves
while I looked elsewhere,
while I bought, and burned, and slept.

Forgive me. No—
don't. Let me hold this ache
the way a mother holds
a child she could not save,
the guilt indistinguishable
from the tenderness,
both of them beating
in the same fist of muscle.

Here, beneath my hand,
is every apology I never made
to the bees, the glaciers,
the last of the loud frogs.
Here is the low green hum
of a planet I love
the way you love someone
already leaving—

too much, too late,
with everything I have,
which is only this:
a heart that will not hold still,
a body that keeps insisting
*love, love, love*
even as the light goes long
and amber
over the dying grass.

I press harder.
I want to feel it fail
and refuse to.
I want to memorize
the shape of caring
this fiercely
for a world
that never asked
to be mourned—

only to be kept.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary confessional prose-poem that blends bodily imagery (a beating heart, blood) with cosmic imagery (spaceships, the Earth bleeding on the sea floor) to explore leaving the planet behind.
counterfactuals.output:
# Departure Velocity

I have been practicing my goodbyes in the mirror, watching the animal
of my heart knock against its cage of ribs like something that wants out,
that has always wanted out, and now the ships are here—

silver as the inside of a wrist, patient as surgeons.

Listen: I was born already leaving. The first cry is a rehearsal
for the last one. Somewhere in me a red tide has been rising since
the beginning, my blood keeping its own countdown, its systole and
its ache, and I have spent thirty years pretending this was living
and not just a slow ascent.

They tell us the Earth is dying. I have seen the footage—
the planet bleeding out on the ocean floor, that dark arterial gush
from a wound we opened looking for something to burn. The sea
turned to a bruise. The reefs went the gray of a stopped pulse.
And still my own heart kept its stubborn drum, kept saying
*here, here, here,* as if here were a place I could stay.

But I have packed my body into a suit the color of forgetting.
I have let them read my vitals like a departure board.
When the engines light I will feel my blood pressed backward,
every cell remembering the direction of gravity one last time
before it lets go, before the great forgetting of weight—

and I want to tell you what it is to leave a world.

It is not triumphant. It is not the flags they show you.
It is looking down through the porthole at the blue-and-white
marble already going small, already becoming a thing you loved
in the past tense, and feeling your own heart—that fist,
that faithful fool—still beating out its little morse
of *home, home, home* to a signal that will not answer.

We took our blood to the stars because we could not stop bleeding.
We left because staying had become a kind of murder we were
committing against the thing that made us. And now the dark
comes up around the ship like water closing over a diver,
and I press my palm to the cold glass, and I feel it there—

the pulse, the pulse, the pulse—

the Earth's last gift, this red machine, still running
long after the planet that wound it has slipped below the horizon
of everything I will ever be able to call * back.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a modern lyric poet about ecological guilt, trusting and distrusting one's own body, and the strange wealth of a self-destructing Earth.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inheritance

I have learned to read the weather
like a bill come due,
each warm December
a small betrayal I participate in
simply by breathing,
by wanting things—
the orange in winter,
the light I leave on
for no one.

My body knows this too,
though I don't trust it.
It tells me it is hungry
and I wonder who paid for that hunger,
what field, what hand,
what distant water table
lowered itself to fill me.

I am afraid of my own appetite
the way you fear
a loyal dog
that once, just once,
showed teeth.

Meanwhile the Earth
keeps spending itself
like an heiress with a terminal diagnosis,
throwing open every window,
letting the heat pour in,
gorgeous and profligate—
the tulips blooming in February,
the sea rising up
to touch the boardwalk
almost tenderly.

There is a wealth in ruin
no one wants to name:
how the last of anything
becomes suddenly precious,
how I've never loved a season
the way I love
this one that shouldn't be here.

And still I wake.
And still the animal of me
insists on continuing,
insists on the coffee,
the commute, the small
electric hum of being alive
at the wrong time,
in the wrong body,
loving it anyway—

this house on fire
I keep calling home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an introspective poem where the narrator recalls seeing a heart beating in a childhood documentary and uses that memory to reflect on mortality, betrayal, and attachment.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Documentary

I was seven when I saw it first—
the heart, unhoused, still working
on a screen too large to look away from.
A muscle, dark and glistening,
opening and closing like a fist
that could not decide
whether to hold or release.

The narrator said something about pumps,
about chambers, about the miracle
of involuntary things.
I remember thinking: *no one asked it to.*
It simply went on, obedient
to a rhythm it never chose,
the way I never chose these hands,
this hunger, this animal insistence
on continuing.

I have carried that image
into every room since—
into the ones where love was promised
and quietly withdrawn,
into the hospital where my grandmother
became a thing that beeped and slowed.
I keep expecting to catch mine
in some act of treason,
to feel it hesitate,
to sense the small conspiracy
already underway inside my chest.

Because that is the betrayal, isn't it—
not the friend who leaves,
not the love that curdles into weather,
but the body's plain refusal
to be permanent.
We are all documentaries
of a thing that will stop.
We are all that muscle,
naked on the table,
doing the only thing we know
until we don't.

And yet—
I have grown fond of the fist,
its stubborn opening,
its unglamorous devotion.
I press my palm against my sternum
some nights, feeling for the proof,
and there it is: *still, still, still,*
attached to nothing but the dark,
in love with a life
it cannot keep,
holding on to me
the only way it can,
which is to say—
by letting go
and gathering again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a meditative, run-on poem addressed to Earth as if saying goodbye, mixing feelings of exhaustion, jealousy, and love, and comparing the speaker to one symptom among billions.
counterfactuals.output:
Goodbye, Earth,

and I mean it the way the tired mean anything, softly, without the strength to slam a door, and I am leaving you the way steam leaves a cup it once was, upward, unbothered, forgetful, and oh how I have loved you, your wet mornings, your dogs asleep in squares of sun, your strangers who held elevators, your rivers that never once asked to be crossed and were crossed anyway, and I am so tired, Earth, tired the way a field is tired after the harvest takes and takes and calls it gratitude, and I confess I am jealous, jealous of the mountains who get to stay, jealous of the patient stones who never had to decide anything, never had to want, jealous of the moon who left you long ago and got to keep watching, got the leaving without the losing, and here I am only a symptom, one ache among your billions of aches, a single fever-dream your body sweats out in the night, a small red mark, a cough, a passing wince you'll forget by morning, and that is fine, that is fine, I never wanted to be the disease, only to be felt, only to be the proof that something living moved through you and mattered for an afternoon, and I am going now the way light goes, which is to say still traveling, still arriving somewhere long after the source has gone dark, and I love you, I love you, I am too exhausted to say it well but I love you, hold the others gently, hold them, I could not stay, I could not stay, thank you for the borrowing, thank you for the brief warm loan of being here at all, goodbye, goodbye, goodbye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
